title: C.A.T.S.: Memory and Control Flow Tracing for Whole-Program Performance Analysis
problem: Performance optimization traditionally focuses on bottleneck-based approaches, but when no apparent bottlenecks exist, engineers lack systematic methods to identify and address whole-program inefficiencies in data layout, sparsity, allocation strategies, and algorithm design.
motivation: Whole-program optimization requires understanding global data access patterns, control flow, and memory behavior. Current profiling tools focus on function-level metrics, missing higher-level performance anti-patterns.
method: C.A.T.S. creates a unified trace that records two things: the program's control flow (the actual sequence of decisions and loops during execution) and every memory access. A compiler analysis automatically extracts these traces from the program's code without running it. Interactive visualizations display this data as timelines, data flow diagrams, and memory access patterns to help engineers identify optimization opportunities in data layout, allocation, and algorithm design.
key_novelty: C.A.T.S. traces control flow (the actual sequence of program decisions and loops) and memory accesses together—rather than just tracking function calls—using static compiler analysis.
contributions: C.A.T.S. tracing format for control flow and memory event capture
Compiler analysis passes for static trace extraction (seconds on consumer hardware)
Interactive timeline, dataflow, and access pattern visualizations
Case studies demonstrating 3x memory footprint reduction and communication-computation overlap improvements
limitations: Evaluation limited to specific application domains; scalability to very large codebases not explored; static extraction accuracy on complex control flow not fully characterized.
